name: Sara Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so you can give me your public answer and your private one. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the city power company out of the Harbour Road depot, mostly on the underground network now, though I still go up poles in the older suburbs. A typical day is opening a pit on a street corner, finding the fault in a cable that's forty years old, and jointing in a new section. I love the puzzle of it, and honestly I love the gadgets, the fault locators, the thermal camera. What wears me out is the traffic, the noise, and kneeling in a wet hole for three hours.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Joining two lengths of cable so the power flows through like it was never cut. You strip back every layer, connect the cores, then build the insulation back up. Get it wrong and it fails in a year, or blows up in your face, so you take your time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I use AI every day and I keep waiting for it to do something big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was still worth having. I use it on my phone to check cable specs, to read old network drawings and to explain a fault to a customer who only speaks Portuguese. Online I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold, and the people selling it should own up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my life stays the same, which isn't bad. I'm fifty-eight, Lena and I want to stop at sixty-three, and the plan works. I'd be a little bored, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I use and keep showing the younger guys tricks with them. Keep our savings growing, we've got about five months put by. Maybe I'd do that online course on network design I've had bookmarked, just for interest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little sigh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd show the younger guys tricks. Which trick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taking a photo of a forty-year-old drawing with coffee stains on it and getting the AI to tell me what cable type it says. Tomasz, he's twenty-six, couldn't believe a grandmother was teaching him that. I'm not a grandmother, but he says I talk like one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust its answers on cable specs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check them against the book every time, at least the first few times for each type. It's been wrong twice that I know of. That's why I still carry the book in the van.

S0.say: I'd say it was still worth having, a good tool that got oversold. I use it every day for cable specs, old drawings and talking to customers in other languages.
S0.think: My life stays the same, which isn't bad, and our plan to stop at sixty-three holds. I'd just be a little bored.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools on the job and teaches younger colleagues how to use them. Keeps building savings of about five months and takes an online course in network design out of interest.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sigh of disappointment.
S0.quote: Tomasz, he's twenty-six, couldn't believe a grandmother was teaching him that.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is the rare older tradesperson who wants AI to do more, not less. She uses it daily but checks it against the book, which shows a practical kind of trust. The hype picture leaves her a little bored rather than relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I think is actually happening. And I'd want to be in front of it, not behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared, not pocketed. If AI makes the company more productive, then crews should get shorter weeks or better pay, and the union should bargain for that now. Online I'd say retraining has to be paid for by the companies and the state, not out of workers' pockets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot. The job's hands-on, and I'm already comfortable with the tools, so I'd be one of the people they ask to try things. My son Jonas tests software for a bank, and he worries me more than I worry about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for any pilot the company runs, new fault-finding systems, digital network maps, whatever. I'd sign up for the union's tech committee and push for training in work time. And I'd tell Jonas to start learning something that needs a body in the room, starting this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit of excitement, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Jonas say when you've raised that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He said, "Mum, you just want me to be an electrician like your mates." Which is true. But he's thinking about it, he asked me last month what an electrician's course costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would struggle with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Henk, he's sixty, never touched a smartphone he could avoid. He's a brilliant jointer, better than me. I'd want the union to make sure the Henks get time and patience, not a test they fail and a letter.

S1.say: I'd say the gains should be shared, through shorter weeks or better pay, and the union should bargain for that now. Retraining should be paid for by companies and the state.
S1.think: I think I'm in a good spot because my job is hands-on and I'm already at ease with the tools. My son, who tests software for a bank, worries me more than my own job does.
S1.do: Volunteers for any company pilot of new tools and joins the union's tech committee to push for training in work time. Encourages her son to start learning a hands-on trade this year.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a bit of excitement.
S1.quote: I'd want the union to make sure the Henks get time and patience, not a test they fail and a letter.
S1.fieldNote: Sara combines early adoption with firm progressive views about sharing gains. She sees herself as a bridge for slower colleagues and names one she admires. Her real worry sits with her son's office job, not her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, with robots. Okay. That's a different thing. That's not a tool anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that we need emergency measures, an income for everyone who loses work, paid by taxing the companies that own the machines. I'd say it at the depot, at the union and online, and I'd be pretty fierce. I'm usually the one cheering for new tech, so people would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my head start doesn't matter much. If a robot can joint a cable in a wet pit, then knowing how to use AI on my phone won't save me. I'd be sixty, three years short of what we planned, and five months of savings is five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away to be one of the people who supervises or trains the robots, because somebody has to at the start. Lena and I would cut the trip to see Mia in Canada and put that money aside. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal for older workers, and I'd start reading about how to make a pension stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, which is strange to admit, but mostly anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said excited. What part excites you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching a machine do a joint perfectly, I'd be fascinated, I can't help it. I'd want to know how it does the stress cone. But I'd feel guilty about being fascinated while Henk's packing his locker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Canada trip, that's about four thousand. Then eating out, and Lena's new bike. We'd keep paying the mortgage early, we've only three years left on it and I want it gone.

S2.say: I'd say we need emergency measures, including an income for everyone who loses work, paid for by taxing the companies that own the machines. People would notice because I'm usually the one cheering for new tech.
S2.think: My head start with AI doesn't matter if a robot can joint a cable in a wet pit. I'd be three years short of our plan with five months of savings.
S2.do: Applies at once to supervise or train the robots, and cancels a four-thousand trip to Canada to save the money. Pushes the union for a deal for older workers and looks into stretching a pension.
S2.feel: Anxious, with an odd and guilty excitement.
S2.quote: I'd feel guilty about being fascinated while Henk's packing his locker.
S2.fieldNote: The fast AGI picture is where Sara's advantage disappears, and she says so plainly. She still moves first, applying to work alongside the robots. The mix of fascination and guilt is the most honest note in her interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to get myself into the right seat, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this decently if we start now. The company should be training crews to run the robots today, and the union should be getting it in writing. Online I'd share anything about schemes that share ownership with workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably be fine. I'd aim to be the person who runs the robot crew for a couple of years, then retire at sixty-three right as it lands. Like I said with the fast one, the head start matters here, because there's time to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a robotics operator course in the evenings, the college on Dock Street has one, about eight months. I'd ask the company to put me on any trial. I'd keep paying the mortgage off early and tell Jonas to finish that electrician's course before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think an electrician's course is safe for Jonas, if robots reach hands-on work by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not safe. Safer than testing bank software, maybe for a few more years. I don't really know, and I'd tell him I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the robotics course cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eighteen hundred, and the union might cover half. I'd pay it myself if not. That's cheaper than the Canada trip and more useful.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do this decently if we start now, with the company training crews to run robots today. I'd share anything about schemes that give workers a share of ownership.
S3.think: I'd probably be fine, running a robot crew for a couple of years and retiring at sixty-three as it lands. My head start matters here because there's time to use it.
S3.do: Takes an eight-month evening robotics operator course costing about eighteen hundred and asks to join company trials. Keeps paying the mortgage down early and urges her son to finish an electrician's course before 2031.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but in a way she feels she can steer.
S3.quote: No, not safe. Safer than testing bank software, maybe for a few more years. I don't really know, and I'd tell him I don't know.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Sara sees a route that ends neatly at retirement. She is honest that the advice she gives her son may not hold. Her plans are concrete and costed, down to the course fee and who might pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'll be sixty-eight and retired. This one's mostly about everybody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and wasting it would be a crime. I'd push for every apprentice to train on robots alongside the old ways. Online I'd say we should be deciding now who owns the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's good, actually. I'd get to see the start of it from the inside and then retire. What I'd worry about is Jonas and Mia at thirty-something, and whether their work's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep using the tools, and maybe do the robotics course in a year or two once it's clearer what kind of robots are coming. I'd stay on the union tech committee until I retire. And I'd vote for whoever's serious about shared ownership and a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said shared ownership. What would that look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The city owns the power company, so the city should own the robots too. Any savings come back as lower bills or a shorter week for everyone. I know that sounds like a dream, but the company used to be fully public, so it's not a crazy idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to tell an apprentice starting this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the cable properly, with your hands, because whoever programs the robots needs someone who knows what a bad joint looks like. And be nice to the machine, it'll be your boss's favourite.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and wasting it would be a crime. Apprentices should train on robots alongside the old ways, and we should decide now who owns the machines.
S4.think: For me it's good, because I'd see the start from the inside and then retire. I'd worry about my grown children in their thirties and whether their work is still there.
S4.do: Keeps working and using AI tools, and plans a robotics course in a year or two once the technology is clearer. Stays on the union tech committee and votes for shared ownership and a basic income.
S4.quote: Be nice to the machine, it'll be your boss's favourite.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gives Sara the outcome she would choose: a front-row seat and then retirement. Her politics come through clearly in the idea that a city-owned company should own its robots. Her humour returns once the pressure is off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes away the one advantage I've got, which is being early. What would help is a basic income that starts the day it lands, paid for by whoever owns the robots, and a proper deal for people my age to go at full pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want to work with them. I would. I'd love one day in a pit with a robot that actually knows what it's doing, then go home and let it finish.

headlineQuote: I'd love one day in a pit with a robot that actually knows what it's doing, then go home and let it finish.
portrait: Sara Schmidt is a fifty-eight-year-old cable jointer and lineworker for the city power company, working out of the Harbour Road depot, who uses AI on her phone every day and teaches younger colleagues to do the same. She shrugs at the hype picture and sees steady change as a chance to lead, while pushing the union to share the gains. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious because it wipes out her head start and lands three years before her planned retirement. With five or ten years she makes costed plans, an evening robotics course and an early mortgage payoff, and her worry moves to her son's office job.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would remove her advantage of being an early adopter and hit before she retires.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income that starts as soon as it lands, paid for by the owners of the robots, and a full-pension exit deal for older workers.
